summary_vn: Cách giới thiệu phở, bún, gỏi cuốn, nước mắm và món ăn Việt cho bạn không phải người Việt.
summary_en: How to introduce phở, bún, gỏi cuốn, fish sauce, and Vietnamese cuisine to non-Vietnamese friends.
regional_note: Phở Bắc nước trong, ít rau; phở Nam đậm hơn, nhiều rau giá. Cả hai đều là phở 'thật' — đừng để bạn bè so sánh kiểu 'cái nào đúng hơn'.

phrases.english: It's pronounced 'fuh' — like the start of 'fun,' with a slight rising tone at the end. Not 'fo.' I won't be picky about it though.
phrases.cultural_note: Most Americans default to 'fo.' A gentle correction is fine; insisting more than once feels prickly. Pick your moment.

phrases.english: Phở comes in two main forms — phở bò is beef broth with rare beef slices, phở gà is chicken. Beef is more common abroad. Both are valid; pick whichever you'd choose at a chicken-soup-vs-beef-soup moment.
phrases.cultural_note: There are also seafood and vegetarian versions. The 'is one more authentic' question is a trap — they're regional and personal.

phrases.vn_moment: Tự gia vị phở — không phải đầu bếp quên
phrases.context: Bạn nước ngoài hỏi vì sao bàn để 1 đống lá và chai sốt.
phrases.english: Vietnamese phở comes with condiments on the side: bean sprouts, basil, lime, chili, and hoisin / sriracha. The chef isn't 'forgetting' to season — you finish the bowl yourself, to your taste.
phrases.cultural_note: Adding everything at once is a beginner move. Start with lime + a pinch of basil, taste, then add. Hoisin and sriracha are personal preference, not required.

phrases.context: Bạn không phải người Việt nhăn mặt khi ngửi mùi.
phrases.english: Fish sauce — nước mắm — is the backbone of Vietnamese flavor. It smells strong on its own but transforms when mixed into a dipping sauce with sugar, lime, garlic, and chili. Don't judge it by the bottle.
phrases.cultural_note: Comparisons to soy sauce miss the point — fish sauce is fermented, salty, and umami-rich. Insulting it ('smells like rot') registers as disrespect even when meant as humor.

phrases.vn_moment: Bánh mì — không chỉ là 'sandwich Việt'
phrases.english: 'Bánh mì' literally just means 'bread' — but the sandwich version uses a French-style baguette stuffed with pâté, cold cuts, pickled carrots, daikon, cilantro, and chili. The French colonial period left us this hybrid.
phrases.cultural_note: Calling it 'just a sandwich' undersells the layering. The pickled vegetables and the herbs are doing real work.

phrases.context: Bạn nước ngoài bối rối hai loại 'spring roll'.
phrases.english: Two different things: 'gỏi cuốn' is the fresh roll — cold, rice paper wrapping shrimp and herbs. 'Chả giò' is the fried roll — crispy, hot. English calls both 'spring roll,' but they're not the same dish.
phrases.cultural_note: Order both at a restaurant if you can — they show different sides of Vietnamese cooking. The fresh roll uses no heat at all; the fried roll uses three different cooking stages.

phrases.context: Khách yêu cầu dao và nĩa khi ăn phở.
phrases.english: Vietnamese food is mostly cut into bite-size pieces in the kitchen, so we eat with chopsticks and a spoon — no knife needed. The spoon is for broth.
phrases.cultural_note: It's fine to ask for a fork if you're not comfortable with chopsticks — most restaurants have them. Asking for a knife signals you weren't sure how the food works.

phrases.vn_moment: Múc nước — đũa và muỗng cùng lúc
phrases.context: Hướng dẫn cách ăn phở bằng đũa và muỗng.
phrases.english: Hold chopsticks in one hand for the noodles and meat, the spoon in the other for the broth. They work together, not in turn. The Western 'finish one then the other' approach makes the bowl go cold.
phrases.cultural_note: Watching a Vietnamese friend eat phở is the easiest tutorial — the two-handed rhythm is hard to describe in words.

phrases.context: Bạn nước ngoài hỏi có nên boa quán nhỏ không.
phrases.english: Street food stalls in Vietnam don't expect tips — the price is the price. Tipping a few thousand đồng won't offend anyone, but it's not the cultural baseline.
phrases.cultural_note: Tipping is creeping into tourist-heavy spots, but it's still optional. Don't feel obligated.

phrases.vn_moment: Mâm cơm gia đình — chia nhau
phrases.context: Khách Mỹ ngạc nhiên vì sao đồ ăn ở giữa bàn.
phrases.english: Vietnamese home meals are family-style — multiple dishes in the center, everyone picks from each. Each person has a small bowl of rice that gets refreshed throughout the meal.
phrases.cultural_note: There's no 'individual plate' default. Eating only from one dish reads as picky. Try a bit of everything — refusing dishes can feel like declining hospitality.

phrases.context: Giải thích vì sao mọi món có cơm.
phrases.english: Rice is the base — almost every Vietnamese home meal includes a bowl of rice per person. The other dishes are 'with rice,' not separate courses.
phrases.cultural_note: Refusing rice ('I'm watching carbs') is fine but mention it ahead of time so the host doesn't feel awkward. Skipping rice is unusual at a family meal.

phrases.context: Phong tục lễ phép ở mâm cơm gia đình.
phrases.english: Before kids start eating, they say 'mời' to each adult at the table — basically 'please eat.' It's a quick acknowledgment that goes person by person.
phrases.cultural_note: If you're a guest at a family meal, watching one round of 'mời' will tell you the household's specific phrasing. Skipping it isn't catastrophic, but joining in earns respect.

phrases.vn_moment: Nước chấm — nhiều loại tùy món
phrases.context: Trên bàn có nhiều bát nước chấm khác nhau.
phrases.english: Different dishes pair with different dipping sauces. The fish-sauce-with-lime-and-chili we use for rolls and grilled meat is different from the soy-and-ginger we use for steamed dishes. The bowl with the dish is the right one.
phrases.cultural_note: Mixing the wrong sauce onto the wrong dish isn't a disaster, but Vietnamese cooks notice. Watch which bowl is closest to which plate.

phrases.vn_moment: Đồ Việt không có phô mai
phrases.context: Đồng nghiệp hỏi 'có phở phô mai không'.
phrases.english: Traditional Vietnamese food doesn't use cheese. There's no phở with cheese, no bánh mì with cheese inside. If you see those in Western Vietnamese restaurants, it's a fusion choice — not authentic.
phrases.cultural_note: This is a genuine gap, not a stylistic one. Dairy isn't a traditional ingredient in Vietnamese cooking.

phrases.context: Đồng nghiệp hỏi vì sao quán phục vụ trà nóng cả mùa hè.
phrases.english: Hot tea — usually unsweetened green or jasmine — gets served before, during, or after the meal. It's the default drink, even in summer. Cold drinks are extras, not the baseline.
phrases.cultural_note: Asking 'do you have iced tea or just hot' is fine — many restaurants serve both. But the hot pot showing up first isn't a mistake.

dialogues.title: Coworker eats phở with you
dialogues.setting: Lunch at a Vietnamese restaurant. Your coworker is trying phở for the first time.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: Wait — what's all this on the side? Bean sprouts, basil, limes... is that for someone else?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: No, that's for you. Vietnamese phở comes plain, and you finish it yourself. Squeeze a wedge of lime in, tear up some basil, then taste before adding more.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: What about the sriracha and the brown sauce?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: That's hoisin. Personal preference — some people love it, others say it kills the broth. Try one drop on a slice of beef and see.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Chopsticks for noodles, spoon for broth. Use them together — that's the rhythm.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Always. Slow down — eating fast is the easy way to burn your mouth on phở.

dialogues.title: Visiting friend at home for dinner
dialogues.setting: You've been invited to a Vietnamese family's home; the host's mom is laying out dishes.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Wait one second — let the elders take rice first. Watch the kids: they say 'mời cô,' 'mời chú,' before they eat. It's a quick round of 'please eat' to each adult.

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.english: Got it. And then I just... pick from the dishes in the middle?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Right. A little bit of everything. The fish on that plate, the morning glory in the bowl, the omelet — sample each. Refusing a dish reads as picky.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: The dipping bowl closest to the dish is the one for that dish. Don't swap them around.

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.english: Okay. Mời cô — did I say that right?
